<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Sirui Chen<sup id="id1" class="ltx_sup">*</sup>
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Yunzhe Qi
</span><span id="id2" class="ltx_note ltx_note_frontmatter ltx_thanks_contribution ltx_role_thanks"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">thanks: </span>Equal Contribution.</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Mengting Ai
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Yifan Sun
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Ruizhong Qiu
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Jiaru Zou
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Jingrui He
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span><span id="id3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">{sirui6, yunzheq2, mai10, yifan50, rq5, jiaruz2, jingrui}@illinois.edu</span>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) relies critically on selecting training data that most benefits model’s downstream performance. Gradient-based data selection methods such as TracIn and Influence Functions leverage influence to identify useful samples, but their computational cost scales poorly, making them impractical for multi-billion-parameter large language models (LLMs).
A common alternative is to use off-the-shelf smaller models as proxies, but they remain suboptimal since their learning dynamics are unclear, their sizes cannot be flexibly adjusted, and they cannot be further aligned with the target model in terms of gradient-based influence estimation.
To address these challenges, we introduce <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span>, a two-stage framework that derives influence-preserving proxies directly from the target model. It first applies a low-rank compression stage to preserve influence information of the target model, and then an aligning stage to align both model gradients and logits, thereby constructing proxies that flexibly control computational cost while retaining the target model’s influence.
Experimental results across diverse LLM families and evaluation tasks show that <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> consistently outperforms off-the-shelf proxies and baseline methods. On Qwen3-4B, a 1.5B proxy constructed with <span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> achieves stronger performance than the larger 1.7B off-the-shelf proxy. Notably, on Llama3.2, <span id="abstract1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> achieves better performance than baselines while reducing computational cost by more than half relative to the full 3B model. These results show that <span id="abstract1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> provides effective influence-preserving proxies, making gradient-based data selection more scalable for LLMs. The code is available at <a href="https://github.com/csr16/IProX" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/csr16/IProX</a></p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<table id="p1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_top">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:0.0pt;height:24.0pt;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"></span></td></tr>

</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h3>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) has become the standard approach for adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) to various downstream tasks. However, the effectiveness of SFT hinges critically on the training data. Prior studies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2023b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024a</a>)</cite> show that naively combining datasets can even degrade downstream performance. The key challenge, therefore, is not the sheer amount of data available but the identification of a curated subset that most effectively enhances model performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A prominent line of work addressing this challenge is gradient-based data selection, where each sample’s importance is estimated through its influence on the model performance. For example, <em id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">TracIn</em> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pruthi et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Han et al., 2023</a>)</cite> estimates the impact of a training sample by accumulating gradient inner products with a validation sample across multiple model checkpoints, while <em id="S1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Influence Functions</em> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koh and Liang, 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kwon et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> approximate the effect of infinitesimally upweighting or downweighting a training sample by scaling its gradient with the inverse Hessian to account for the local curvature of the loss landscape. Despite their success, both methods impose substantial computational overhead, requiring either the storage of numerous checkpoints with repeated backpropagation or the computation of costly inverse-Hessian vector products. This overhead scales poorly with model size, making these methods impractical for multi-billion-parameter LLMs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grosse et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">While there are some efforts focusing on simplifying the influence computation itself <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kwon et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2025c</a>)</cite>, we pivot to an alternative, orthogonal question:
<span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">can the expensive influence calculation for a target model be effectively offloaded to a smaller, cost-effective proxy model?</span>
The idea of using smaller models to predict the behavior of larger ones is already prevalent, most notably through scaling laws that estimate a target model’s performance from its smaller counterparts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kaplan et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shum et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zeng et al., </a>; <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zou et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>.
Motivated by this, we explore whether this proxy paradigm can also be extended to data selection by leveraging gradient-based influence scores from smaller models as approximations for larger ones, thereby mitigating the prohibitive cost of full-scale computation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">A direct strategy is to use off-the-shelf proxy models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, such as applying Llama3-8B to select data for Llama3-70B. These proxies provide strong baselines and useful guidance, but remain suboptimal for three main reasons. First, while their task performance is usually reported, much less is known about their learning dynamics on the data. As a result, choosing an off-the-shelf proxy for gradient-based influence estimation typically relies on prior knowledge (e.g., assuming the larger model always behaves similarly to its smaller counterparts), without a clear understanding of how much benefit is gained by increasing size. Second, the available off-the-shelf models within each family are restricted to a handful of fixed sizes, which limits flexibility in adjusting proxy capacity to different computational budgets. Third—and most importantly, there is no systematic way to better align these proxies with the target model for influence estimation.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_center ltx_align_floatright" style="width:27%;">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>For Qwen3-4B, a 1.5B <span id="S1.F1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> outperforms the Qwen3-1.7B off-the-shelf proxy, demonstrating that a smaller influence-pre-serving proxy can achieve better data selection performance.</figcaption><img src="2602.17835v1/teaser.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:154/138;" width="154" height="138" alt="Refer to caption">
</figure>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">To address these challenges, we propose <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span>, a principled two-stage framework that constructs a proxy directly from the target model, starting with compression and followed by alignment.
The key idea is straightforward: instead of relying on a smaller model with assumed preferences, we derive a smaller model directly from the target so that it inherits the gradient characteristics of the original. This design provides flexibility in controlling computational cost and, more importantly, establishes a principled path to preserve the influence of the target model. Concretely, we first employ <em id="S1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Influence-Preserving Singular Value Decomposition (IPSVD)</em>, where each weight matrix of the target model is compressed to retain components most relevant for gradient-based influence.
Building on this, we then introduce an <em id="S1.p5.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">aligning stage</em> that refines the proxy by matching its gradients to those of the target model within the low-rank space while anchoring its output logits to remain consistent. Together, these stages yield a proxy that is both efficient and tailored for gradient-based data selection.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Experimental results demonstrate that <span id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> achieves consistently better performance than off-the-shelf proxies across diverse tasks and model families, and its advantages hold under different gradient-based influence estimators.
A representative example is shown in Fig. <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, where for the Qwen3-4B target model, our 1.5B proxy constructed by <span id="S1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> surpasses a larger 1.7B off-the-shelf proxy in average performance, highlighting that a smaller <span id="S1.p6.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> can outperform larger off-the-shelf ones. In addition to stronger performance, <span id="S1.p6.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> is efficient. In our experiments on Llama3.2, it reduces the computational overhead by more than half relative to the full 3B model, offering a practical and scalable path for efficient gradient-based data selection in LLM fine-tuning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Works</h3>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Gradient-Based Data Selection.</span>  Traditional data selection is often <em id="S2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">model-agnostic</em>, emphasizing dataset structure such as diversity <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, redundancy reduction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2015</a>)</cite>, or similarity to a target distribution <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kang et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>. In contrast, <em id="S2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">gradient-based</em> selection is <em id="S2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">model-aware</em>, leveraging first- and second-order training dynamics to estimate each example’s impact on learning and validation performance. A main line builds on <em id="S2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">influence functions</em> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kwon et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grosse et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Klochkov and Liu, 2024</a>)</cite>, which approximate the leave-one-out effect of upweighting or removing a training example, helping identify high-impact data points with respect to a target distribution.
Another complementary line uses <em id="S2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">training-dynamics</em> attribution <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bae et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, scoring examples by how their gradients align with improvements on held-out targets across training checkpoints. A representative approach is TracIn <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pruthi et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Han et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, which aggregates such gradient-similarity signals along the optimization trajectory, avoiding expensive second-order computations while remaining model-aware.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Efficient Data Selection for LLMs.</span>  With the growing size of LLMs, gradient-based data selection has become increasingly impractical, motivating more efficient adaptations. Some works reduce the cost of influence estimation by simplifying second-order derivatives <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kwon et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grosse et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, while others compute influences on a small subset and extrapolate to the full dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2025c</a>)</cite>. Recently, an alternative line of work has explored using smaller off-the-shelf proxy models to guide data selection for larger ones, though these approaches primarily rely on loss signals rather than exploiting gradient information <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shum et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. In the broader context of efficient LLM adaptation, recent studies also leverage fine-tuning dynamics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zeng et al., </a>)</cite> and automated scaling laws <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2025b</a>)</cite> to optimize computational allocation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LLM Compression via Decomposition Methods.</span>  Decomposition-based compression exploits the low intrinsic rank of weight matrices. Early work showed that singular value decomposition (SVD) can effectively approximate transformer layers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ganesh et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. Subsequent studies refined this idea: ASVD incorporates neuron activation patterns <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yuan et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, CALDERA combines low-rank factorization with quantization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Saha et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and MoDeGPT applies Nyström approximation to entire transformer blocks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>. SVD-based strategies have also been extended to Mixture-of-Experts models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ai et al., 2025c</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Additionally, ShortGPT introduces an importance-scoring mechanism to identify and retain the most critical layers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Men et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Preliminaries and Problem Definition</h3>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We consider a candidate training dataset <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}</annotation></semantics></math> and a target validation dataset <math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}</annotation></semantics></math>, which may either follow the same distribution or a different one. The objective of <em id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">model-aware data selection</em> is to identify a subset <math id="S3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}^{*}\subseteq\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>⊆</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}^{*}\subseteq\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}</annotation></semantics></math> with a fixed budget <math id="S3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> such that fine-tuning a model <math id="S3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> on <math id="S3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> maximizes its downstream performance on <math id="S3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}^{*}\;=\;\underset{\mathcal{D}\subseteq\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}},\,|\mathcal{D}|=k}{\arg\max}\;\mathbb{E}_{z^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}}\big[\mathcal{U}(f_{\theta(\mathcal{D})};z^{\prime})\big]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0.558em" rspace="0.558em">=</mo><mrow><munder accentunder="true"><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>max</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.700em">𝒟</mi><mo mathsize="0.700em">⊆</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.700em">𝒟</mi><mtext mathsize="0.710em">train</mtext></msub></mrow><mo mathsize="0.700em" rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><mo maxsize="0.700em" minsize="0.700em" stretchy="true">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.700em">𝒟</mi><mo maxsize="0.700em" minsize="0.700em" stretchy="true">|</mo></mrow><mo mathsize="0.700em">=</mo><mi mathsize="0.700em">k</mi></mrow></mrow></munder><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">[</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}^{*}\;=\;\underset{\mathcal{D}\subseteq\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}},\,|\mathcal{D}|=k}{\arg\max}\;\mathbb{E}_{z^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}}\big[\mathcal{U}(f_{\theta(\mathcal{D})};z^{\prime})\big],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{U}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{U}</annotation></semantics></math> is a task utility (e.g., accuracy), <math id="S3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta(\mathcal{D})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta(\mathcal{D})</annotation></semantics></math> are the model parameters fine-tuned on <math id="S3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math>,
and <math id="S3.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}</annotation></semantics></math> is a validation sample.
Directly solving the combinatorial optimization in Eq. <a href="#S3.E1" title="In 3 Preliminaries and Problem Definition ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> is intractable. A widely used strategy is to instead score each training sample <math id="S3.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}</annotation></semantics></math> based on its <em id="S3.p1.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">gradient-based influence</em> on <math id="S3.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}</annotation></semantics></math> and select the top-<math id="S3.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> samples. This is typically achieved by defining a pairwise influence score <math id="S3.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I(z,z^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I(z,z^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math>, which quantifies the utility of training on a sample <math id="S3.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math> for the model’s performance on a target sample <math id="S3.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A prominent example of this idea is <em id="S3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">TracIn</em> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pruthi et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, which approximates <math id="S3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I(z,z^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I(z,z^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math> by accumulating gradient similarities between training and target samples over multiple checkpoints:</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{\text{TracIn}}(z,z^{\prime})=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}\langle\nabla_{\theta}L(z;\theta_{t}),\nabla_{\theta}L(z^{\prime};\theta_{t})\rangle," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mtext>TracIn</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></munderover><mrow><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>θ</mi></msub><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>θ</mi></msub><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{\text{TracIn}}(z,z^{\prime})=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}\langle\nabla_{\theta}L(z;\theta_{t}),\nabla_{\theta}L(z^{\prime};\theta_{t})\rangle,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L(\cdot\,;\ \cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L(\cdot\,;\ \cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> is the loss function, <math id="S3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is the model’s parameters at checkpoint <math id="S3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>η</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is the averaged learning rate in iteration <math id="S3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>. By probing the geometry of the loss landscape throughout training, this method provides a faithful measure of a sample’s utility. Another seminal method, <em id="S3.p2.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Influence Functions</em> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koh and Liang, 2017</a>)</cite>, estimates the influence of a training sample by modeling how the final model parameters would change if that sample were infinitesimally upweighted. This parameter change is approximated as the inverse Hessian of the loss multiplied by the sample’s gradient.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">However, the computational cost of these gradient-based methods is prohibitive for large-scale models, motivating the use of smaller proxies to approximate influence scores. The central challenge, and the focus of this work, is to design a proxy model <math id="S3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta^{\prime}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta^{\prime}}</annotation></semantics></math> that not only approximates the influence scores of the target model <math id="S3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> but also strikes a balance between efficiency and selection quality. Ideally, the proxy should be small enough to offer notable computational savings while remaining sufficiently aligned with the target model to guide effective data selection.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17835v1/main_fig.png" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:428/162;" width="428" height="162" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Overview of <span id="S3.F2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span>. In the first stage (left), <em id="S3.F2.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">IPSVD</em> leverages hidden states and gradients to build second-moment matrices that reweight the model weights for proxy initialization. In the second stage (right), the proxy is further aligned with the target LLM through internal gradient alignment in the low-rank space and external logits anchoring for stability.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Proxy Construction via Influence-Preserving Compression</h3>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce <span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span>, summarized in Fig. <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 Preliminaries and Problem Definition ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, which consists of two stages. The first stage compresses the model with an influence-preserving SVD (§<a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 Stage 1: Influence-Preserving SVD ‣ 4 Proxy Construction via Influence-Preserving Compression ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>) that uses second-moment reweighting to retain influence-relevant components. The second stage aligns the proxy with the target LLM (§<a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 Stage 2: Approximate Gradient Alignment in the Weight Space ‣ 4 Proxy Construction via Influence-Preserving Compression ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>) by matching gradients in the low-rank space and anchoring the logits distribution for stability.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Stage 1: Influence-Preserving SVD</h4>

<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_center ltx_align_floatright" style="width:30%;">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Loss and influence (TracIn) retention of SVD and our IPSVD under different compression sparsity.</figcaption><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17835v1/retention_vs_sparsity_svd_iprox.svg" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:165/143;" width="165" height="143"></object>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Limitation of Standard SVD.</span> We begin by describing how the proxy model is initialized. A natural approach is to compress the model via low-rank approximation of its weight matrices. For any weight matrix <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}</annotation></semantics></math> in the target model <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n,m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n,m</annotation></semantics></math> are output and input dimensions, we can approximate it as <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W\approx AB" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W\approx AB</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times m}</annotation></semantics></math>. The rank <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r\ll\min(n,m)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>≪</mo><mrow><mi>min</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r\ll\min(n,m)</annotation></semantics></math> directly controls the size of the resulting proxy model, with lower ranks corresponding to higher model sparsity. The standard method for such decomposition is Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), which yields the optimal rank-<math id="S4.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> approximation under the Frobenius reconstruction error objective <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Eckart and Young, 1936</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Golub and Van Loan, 2013</a>)</cite>. However, this objective is misaligned with our goal of data selection, since minimizing reconstruction error provides no guarantee that the proxy model will preserve the gradient-based influence of the target model.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As illustrated in Fig. <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.1 Stage 1: Influence-Preserving SVD ‣ 4 Proxy Construction via Influence-Preserving Compression ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, when a 4-layer MLP is compressed on a synthetic classification task using standard SVD, <em id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">loss retention</em> (measured as the ratio between the original and compressed losses) remains relatively stable when the sparsity is low, while <em id="S4.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">influence retention</em> (measured by Spearman correlation with the oracle influence) deteriorates much more rapidly. These observations highlight the need for a compression method that explicitly preserves influence.
To this end, our IPSVD is designed to retain influence-relevant components. As previewed in Fig. <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.1 Stage 1: Influence-Preserving SVD ‣ 4 Proxy Construction via Influence-Preserving Compression ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, IPSVD attains markedly higher influence retention than standard SVD while maintaining comparable loss retention across sparsity levels. We now present the technical details.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">IPSVD with Reweighting.</span> Our goal is to construct a compressed proxy whose influence scores approximate those of the target model. For clarity, we focus on a simplified variant of the TracIn computed from a single checkpoint and denote it as <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>I</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I</annotation></semantics></math>, omitting the subscript.
Without loss of generality, we present the analysis with TracIn, and the results also apply to other gradient-based methods such as Influence Functions (see Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Influence-Preserving Low-Rank Approximation for Influence Functions ‣ Appendix ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>).
Specifically, for a weight matrix <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> at layer <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math>, its gradient is given by the outer product <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{W_{\ell}}L(z;\theta)=\delta_{\ell}(z)h_{\ell-1}(z)^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></msub><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{W_{\ell}}L(z;\theta)=\delta_{\ell}(z)h_{\ell-1}(z)^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{\ell-1}(z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{\ell-1}(z)</annotation></semantics></math> is the input to layer <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta_{\ell}(z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta_{\ell}(z)</annotation></semantics></math> is the upstream gradient from the loss. Then the influence of <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> is:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{W_{\ell}}(z,z^{\prime})=\langle\nabla_{W_{\ell}}L(z;\theta),\nabla_{W_{\ell}}L(z^{\prime};\theta)\rangle_{F}=\langle\delta_{\ell}(z),\delta_{\ell}(z^{\prime})\rangle_{F}\langle stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo h_{\ell-1}(z),h_{\ell-1}(z^{\prime})\rangle_{F}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{F}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{F}</annotation></semantics></math> is Frobenius inner product.
From this definition, we observe that any sufficiently small perturbation <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\ell}\mapsto\widehat{W}_{\ell}=W_{\ell}+E_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">↦</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>W</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\ell}\mapsto\widehat{W}_{\ell}=W_{\ell}+E_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> affects the influence only through the resulting changes <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta_{\ell}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta_{\ell}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math>. A first-order Taylor expansion of the loss with respect to <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> in the direction of the perturbation <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> yields the scalar <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\langle\nabla_{W_{\ell}}L(z;\theta),E_{\ell}\rangle_{F}=\delta_{\ell}(z)^{\top}E_{\ell}h_{\ell-1}(z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></msub><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\langle\nabla_{W_{\ell}}L(z;\theta),E_{\ell}\rangle_{F}=\delta_{\ell}(z)^{\top}E_{\ell}h_{\ell-1}(z)</annotation></semantics></math>, which captures the effect of the perturbation on the sample loss. We therefore define the <em id="S4.SS1.p3.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">layer-local directional effect</em> of a perturbation <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> on a sample <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math> as:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>

<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The following proposition provides a theoretical justification
for using the expected squared effect, <math id="S4.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}_{z}[e_{\ell}(z)^{2}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>z</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}_{z}[e_{\ell}(z)^{2}]</annotation></semantics></math>, as a tractable surrogate
for preserving the influence score.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_proposition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S4.Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proposition 4.1</span></span><span id="S4.Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S4.Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Consider a perturbation to layer <math id="S4.Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math>: <math id="S4.Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\ell}\mapsto\widehat{W}_{\ell}=W_{\ell}+E_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">↦</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>W</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\ell}\mapsto\widehat{W}_{\ell}=W_{\ell}+E_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math>. Under assumptions of local smoothness, geometric coherence, and a bounded covariate shift condition between the distributions of <math id="S4.Thmtheorem1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.Thmtheorem1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> (see Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Proof of Proposition ‣ Appendix ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a> for details), there exists a data-dependent constant <math id="S4.Thmtheorem1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{\kappa}&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>κ</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{\kappa}&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> such that the expected change in the influence contribution is bounded by:</span></p>
<table id="S4.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}_{z,z^{\prime}}\big|I_{\widehat{W}_{\ell}}(z,z^{\prime})-I_{W_{\ell}}(z,z^{\prime})\big|\;\leq\;C_{\kappa}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{z}\!\left[e_{\ell}(z)^{2}\right]}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" stretchy="true">|</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>W</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" rspace="0.280em" stretchy="true">|</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.558em">≤</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>κ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>z</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}_{z,z^{\prime}}\big|I_{\widehat{W}_{\ell}}(z,z^{\prime})-I_{W_{\ell}}(z,z^{\prime})\big|\;\leq\;C_{\kappa}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{z}\!\left[e_{\ell}(z)^{2}\right]}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
