</div>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The proof is deferred to Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Proof of Proposition ‣ Appendix ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>.
Intuitively, the smoothness assumption ensures that perturbations in layer weights
translate into proportionally bounded changes in the gradients.
The error term <math id="S4.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e_{\ell}(z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e_{\ell}(z)</annotation></semantics></math> represents the local gradient deviation caused by <math id="S4.SS1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math>,
and its squared expectation thus serves as a surrogate for bounding the discrepancy
in pairwise influence <math id="S4.SS1.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{W_{\ell}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{W_{\ell}}</annotation></semantics></math> across samples.
Minimizing <math id="S4.SS1.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}_{z}[e_{\ell}(z)^{2}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>z</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}_{z}[e_{\ell}(z)^{2}]</annotation></semantics></math> therefore directly controls the distortion
of the influences.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Building on this result, our goal is to find the optimal low-rank approximation <math id="S4.SS1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widehat{W}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>W</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widehat{W}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> that minimizes the expected squared effect, <math id="S4.SS1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}_{z}[e_{\ell}(z)^{2}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>z</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}_{z}[e_{\ell}(z)^{2}]</annotation></semantics></math>.
This objective can be expressed as a weighted Frobenius norm between the original and compressed weights, which under the K-FAC approximation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Martens and Grosse, 2015</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grosse and Martens, 2016</a>)</cite> takes the following form:</p>
<table id="S4.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\min_{\widehat{W}_{\ell}}\mathbb{E}_{z}\left[e_{\ell}(z)^{2}\right]\approx\;\min_{\widehat{W}_{\ell}}\left\|C_{\delta,\ell}^{1/2}(W_{\ell}-\widehat{W}_{\ell})C_{h,\ell}^{1/2}\right\|_{F}^{2}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><munder><mi>min</mi><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>W</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></munder><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>z</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.558em">≈</mo><mrow><munder><mi>min</mi><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>W</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></munder><mo>⁡</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>W</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\min_{\widehat{W}_{\ell}}\mathbb{E}_{z}\left[e_{\ell}(z)^{2}\right]\approx\;\min_{\widehat{W}_{\ell}}\left\|C_{\delta,\ell}^{1/2}(W_{\ell}-\widehat{W}_{\ell})C_{h,\ell}^{1/2}\right\|_{F}^{2},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS1.p6.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS1.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{h,\ell}\triangleq\mathbb{E}[h_{\ell-1}h_{\ell-1}^{\top}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow></msub><mo>≜</mo><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{h,\ell}\triangleq\mathbb{E}[h_{\ell-1}h_{\ell-1}^{\top}]</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{\delta,\ell}\triangleq\mathbb{E}[\delta_{\ell}\delta_{\ell}^{\top}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow></msub><mo>≜</mo><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>δ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{\delta,\ell}\triangleq\mathbb{E}[\delta_{\ell}\delta_{\ell}^{\top}]</annotation></semantics></math> are the second moment matrices of the inputs and upstream gradients, respectively.
In effect, these matrices form a reweighting scheme. They rescale <math id="S4.SS1.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> to more heavily penalize errors in directions where inputs are typically large (identified by <math id="S4.SS1.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{h,\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{h,\ell}</annotation></semantics></math>) and where the loss is most sensitive (identified by <math id="S4.SS1.p6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{\delta,\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{\delta,\ell}</annotation></semantics></math>). This ensures that our approximation prioritizes preserving the weights most critical to the influences.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">This reweighting can be expressed by the data-dependent matrix
<math id="S4.SS1.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{\ell}\triangleq C_{\delta,\ell}^{1/2}W_{\ell}C_{h,\ell}^{1/2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>≜</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{\ell}\triangleq C_{\delta,\ell}^{1/2}W_{\ell}C_{h,\ell}^{1/2}</annotation></semantics></math>.
We then compute the SVD of this matrix, <math id="S4.SS1.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{\ell}=U_{\ell}\Sigma_{\ell}V_{\ell}^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{\ell}=U_{\ell}\Sigma_{\ell}V_{\ell}^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math>, and truncate it to the top <math id="S4.SS1.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>r</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> singular values to obtain the components <math id="S4.SS1.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="U_{\ell,r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>U</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">U_{\ell,r}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS1.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma_{\ell,r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma_{\ell,r}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S4.SS1.p7.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{\ell,r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>V</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{\ell,r}</annotation></semantics></math>. The optimal low-rank approximation <math id="S4.SS1.p7.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widehat{W}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>W</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widehat{W}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> is then constructed by transforming these truncated components back to the original weight space:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\widehat{W}_{\ell}=C_{\delta,\ell}^{-1/2}(U_{\ell,r}\Sigma_{\ell,r}V_{\ell,r}^{\top})C_{h,\ell}^{-1/2}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>W</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widehat{W}_{\ell}=C_{\delta,\ell}^{-1/2}(U_{\ell,r}\Sigma_{\ell,r}V_{\ell,r}^{\top})C_{h,\ell}^{-1/2}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS1.p7.2" class="ltx_p">For implementation, this is directly decomposed into the low-rank matrices <math id="S4.SS1.p7.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widehat{W}_{\ell}=A_{\ell}B_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>W</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widehat{W}_{\ell}=A_{\ell}B_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.SS1.p7.m9" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="A_{\ell}=C_{\delta,\ell}^{-1/2}U_{\ell,r}\Sigma_{\ell,r}^{1/2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>U</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{\ell}=C_{\delta,\ell}^{-1/2}U_{\ell,r}\Sigma_{\ell,r}^{1/2}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.p7.m10" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="B_{\ell}=\Sigma_{\ell,r}^{1/2}V_{\ell,r}^{\top}C_{h,\ell}^{-1/2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mi>V</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mi>C</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{\ell}=\Sigma_{\ell,r}^{1/2}V_{\ell,r}^{\top}C_{h,\ell}^{-1/2}</annotation></semantics></math>.
To ensure numerical stability, we add a small damping term <math id="S4.SS1.p7.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda I" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>I</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda I</annotation></semantics></math> to each second moment matrix. In this low-rank approximation, the weight matrix <math id="S4.SS1.p7.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{\ell}\times n_{\ell}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{\ell}\times n_{\ell}}</annotation></semantics></math> is approximated with two smaller matrices, <math id="S4.SS1.p7.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{\ell}\times r_{\ell}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{\ell}\times r_{\ell}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.p7.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{r_{\ell}\times n_{\ell}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{r_{\ell}\times n_{\ell}}</annotation></semantics></math>, reducing the parameters at layer <math id="S4.SS1.p7.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS1.p7.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{\ell}(m_{\ell}+n_{\ell})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{\ell}(m_{\ell}+n_{\ell})</annotation></semantics></math>. The rank <math id="S4.SS1.p7.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>r</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> provides flexible control over the proxy size, enabling a balance between efficiency and approximation quality under a given computational budget.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Efficient and Scalable Implementation.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Computing the square roots and inverses of the large second moment matrices <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{h,\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{h,\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{\delta,\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{\delta,\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> is prohibitively expensive for large models. To avoid forming these matrices, we approximate the second-moment statistics using a small<span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">probe set</span> of <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> samples. A single forward and backward pass collects the inputs and gradients at each layer <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math>, which are then used to form two matrices:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{\ell}=[h_{\ell-1}(z_{1}),\dots,h_{\ell-1}(z_{N})]\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\ell}\times N}\quad\text{and}\quad\Delta_{\ell}=[\delta_{\ell}(z_{1}),\dots,\delta_{\ell}(z_{N})]\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{\ell}\times N}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mtext>and</mtext><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{\ell}=[h_{\ell-1}(z_{1}),\dots,h_{\ell-1}(z_{N})]\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\ell}\times N}\quad\text{and}\quad\Delta_{\ell}=[\delta_{\ell}(z_{1}),\dots,\delta_{\ell}(z_{N})]\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{\ell}\times N}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Instead of building the full second moment matrices (e.g., <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{h,\ell}\approx\frac{1}{N}H_{\ell}H_{\ell}^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow></msub><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{h,\ell}\approx\frac{1}{N}H_{\ell}H_{\ell}^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math>), we compute the "skinny" SVDs of these tall-and-thin probe matrices directly: <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{\ell}=U_{H,\ell}\Sigma_{H,\ell}V_{H,\ell}^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{\ell}=U_{H,\ell}\Sigma_{H,\ell}V_{H,\ell}^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{\ell}=U_{\Delta,\ell}\Sigma_{\Delta,\ell}V_{\Delta,\ell}^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{\ell}=U_{\Delta,\ell}\Sigma_{\Delta,\ell}V_{\Delta,\ell}^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math>.
This decomposition provides the key to bypassing the expensive computation. The SVD of the large, re-weighted matrix <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> can be almost entirely constructed from the SVD of a much smaller <em id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">core matrix</em>, which is built using the components of our skinny SVDs. This reduces the problem to finding the SVD of a matrix whose dimensions are at most <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N\times N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N\times N</annotation></semantics></math>, a dramatically smaller task. The complexity is then reduced from <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(n_{\ell}^{3}+m_{\ell}^{3})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>3</mn></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>3</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(n_{\ell}^{3}+m_{\ell}^{3})</annotation></semantics></math> for full eigen-decompositions to <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(N^{3}+n_{\ell}N^{2}+m_{\ell}N^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>N</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>N</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>N</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(N^{3}+n_{\ell}N^{2}+m_{\ell}N^{2})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N\ll n_{\ell},m_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>≪</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N\ll n_{\ell},m_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math>. For a complete derivation, please see Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Efficient Implementation via Probe-Based Approximation and Core SVD ‣ Appendix ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Stage 2: Approximate Gradient Alignment in the Weight Space</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The initial proxy model <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta^{\prime}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta^{\prime}}</annotation></semantics></math> adheres to the theoretical bound established in Proposition <a href="#S4.Thmtheorem1" title="Proposition 4.1. ‣ 4.1 Stage 1: Influence-Preserving SVD ‣ 4 Proxy Construction via Influence-Preserving Compression ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>. However, as approximation errors compound across layers, its alignment in terms of influence preserving with the original model <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> should still be refined. To this end, we employ an aligning stage wherein the proxy is trained to directly mimic the gradient responses signals of the target model.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Aligning Internal Gradient via Low-Rank Projection.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our goal is to align the gradients of the initialized proxy with those of the target model. A direct comparison of their gradients, <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{\theta^{\prime}}L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub><mi>L</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{\theta^{\prime}}L</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{\theta}L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>θ</mi></msub><mi>L</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{\theta}L</annotation></semantics></math>, is ill-posed due to the dimensional mismatch between the models. In practice, this can be addressed by projecting the proxy’s gradient into the original model’s high-dimensional weight space. For instance, for any layer <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> and a given batch <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{B}=\{z_{i}\}_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{B}|}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{B}=\{z_{i}\}_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{B}|}</annotation></semantics></math>, one can reconstruct the proxy gradient <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{W^{\prime}_{\ell}}L(\mathcal{B};\theta^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup></msub><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{W^{\prime}_{\ell}}L(\mathcal{B};\theta^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math> and minimize its distance to the target gradient <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{W_{\ell}}L(\mathcal{B};\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></msub><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{W_{\ell}}L(\mathcal{B};\theta)</annotation></semantics></math>. However, this approach has a critical drawback. Once we align the gradients of <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{\prime}_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{\prime}_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> in the full parameter space, any subsequent influence calculation would also require reconstructing the proxy’s gradient in this high-dimensional form. Performing this reconstruction for each sample introduces substantial computational and memory overhead, which undermines the efficiency benefits of a low-rank proxy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To ensure the proxy remains efficient for downstream tasks, we adopt a more practical strategy: we project the original model’s gradient <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">down</span> into the low-rank proxy space and perform the alignment there. Since the proxy layer is defined by low-rank matrices <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> (where <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\ell}\approx A_{\ell}B_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>≈</mo><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\ell}\approx A_{\ell}B_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math>), its true gradients are with respect to these matrices, <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{A_{\ell}}L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></msub><mi>L</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{A_{\ell}}L</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{B_{\ell}}L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></msub><mi>L</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{B_{\ell}}L</annotation></semantics></math>. Using the chain rule, we can project the full gradient <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{W_{\ell}}L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></msub><mi>L</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{W_{\ell}}L</annotation></semantics></math> onto <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{A_{\ell}}L=\frac{\partial L}{\partial W_{\ell}}\frac{\partial W_{\ell}}{\partial A_{\ell}}=\nabla_{W_{\ell}}LB_{\ell}^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></msub><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></msub><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{A_{\ell}}L=\frac{\partial L}{\partial W_{\ell}}\frac{\partial W_{\ell}}{\partial A_{\ell}}=\nabla_{W_{\ell}}LB_{\ell}^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{B_{\ell}}L=\frac{\partial L}{\partial W_{\ell}}\frac{\partial W_{\ell}}{\partial B_{\ell}}=A_{\ell}^{\top}\nabla_{W_{\ell}}L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></msub><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></msub><mi>L</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{B_{\ell}}L=\frac{\partial L}{\partial W_{\ell}}\frac{\partial W_{\ell}}{\partial B_{\ell}}=A_{\ell}^{\top}\nabla_{W_{\ell}}L</annotation></semantics></math>. This yields a loss based on the following alignment objectives:</p>
<table id="S4.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{\mathrm{GA}}(\mathcal{B};\theta^{\prime})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{L}|}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}}\left(d(\nabla_{A_{\ell}}L,\text{sg}(\nabla_{W_{\ell}}L)B_{\ell}^{\top})+d(\nabla_{B_{\ell}}L,A_{\ell}^{\top}\text{sg}(\nabla_{W_{\ell}}L))\right)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>GA</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow></munder><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></msub><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mtext>sg</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></msub><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></msub><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>sg</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></msub><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{\mathrm{GA}}(\mathcal{B};\theta^{\prime})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{L}|}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}}\left(d(\nabla_{A_{\ell}}L,\text{sg}(\nabla_{W_{\ell}}L)B_{\ell}^{\top})+d(\nabla_{B_{\ell}}L,A_{\ell}^{\top}\text{sg}(\nabla_{W_{\ell}}L))\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d(\cdot,\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d(\cdot,\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> is a distance function and <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes all decomposed layers in the proxy model.
Here <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{sg}(\nabla_{W_{\ell}}L)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>sg</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></msub><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{sg}(\nabla_{W_{\ell}}L)</annotation></semantics></math> indicates stop gradient.
This objective aligns the gradients entirely within the parameter space of the proxy, eliminating any need for high-dimensional reconstruction during influence calculation and thus preserving its efficiency.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Anchoring External Output Behavior.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To stabilize gradient alignment and prevent the proxy from collapsing, we anchor its output distribution to that of the teacher model, inspired by the idea of knowledge distillation. This provides a stable basis for alignment, where we employ the standard forward Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence loss:</p>
<table id="S4.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E7.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="L_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathcal{B};\theta^{\prime})\;=\;\tau^{2}\;\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}|}\sum_{z\in\mathcal{B}}\,\mathrm{KL}\!\left(\mathrm{softmax}\big(f_{\theta}(z)/\tau\big)\,\big\|\,\mathrm{softmax}\big(f_{\theta^{\prime}}(z)/\tau\big)\right)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>KL</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mo>;</mo><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo rspace="0.280em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.558em">=</mo><msup><mi>τ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi></mrow></munder><mpadded style="width:1.431em;" width="1.431em"><mi>KL</mi></mpadded><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>softmax</mi><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" mathsize="1.200em" rspace="0.337em">∥</mo><mi>softmax</mi><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathcal{B};\theta^{\prime})\;=\;\tau^{2}\;\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}|}\sum_{z\in\mathcal{B}}\,\mathrm{KL}\!\left(\mathrm{softmax}\big(f_{\theta}(z)/\tau\big)\,\big\|\,\mathrm{softmax}\big(f_{\theta^{\prime}}(z)/\tau\big)\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> is the distillation temperature and <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta},f_{\theta^{\prime}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta},f_{\theta^{\prime}}</annotation></semantics></math> are output logits.
Our final objective for the initialized proxy combines the gradient alignment and output anchoring losses:</p>
<table id="S4.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\min_{\theta^{\prime}}\;L_{\mathrm{GA}}(\mathcal{B};\theta^{\prime})\;+\;\lambda_{\mathrm{KL}}\;L_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathcal{B};\theta^{\prime})," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><munder><mi>min</mi><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></munder><mo lspace="0.447em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>GA</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo rspace="0.280em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.502em">+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>KL</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>KL</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\min_{\theta^{\prime}}\;L_{\mathrm{GA}}(\mathcal{B};\theta^{\prime})\;+\;\lambda_{\mathrm{KL}}\;L_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathcal{B};\theta^{\prime}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{\mathrm{KL}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>KL</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{\mathrm{KL}}</annotation></semantics></math> controls the strength of the anchoring term.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Discussion.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> shows that low-rank proxies can preserve gradient-based influences, but there are trade-offs to consider. The embedding layer and LM head are essential for model performance and are less suitable for compression <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Namburi et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dettmers et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, which places a natural limit on parameter reduction. Moreover, prior work finds that model quality drops sharply once the rank falls below about 10% of the original size <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hsu et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, meaning proxies cannot be reduced arbitrarily without sacrificing performance or their ability to preserve influence. Even with our aligning stage, fully recovering gradient behavior under such aggressive compression remains difficult. These limitations do not diminish the usefulness of our method but highlight the inherent trade-offs between efficiency and proxy quality. Further discussion is provided in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Further Discussion ‣ Appendix ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Experiments</h3>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we provide a comprehensive evaluation of <span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span>.
We first describe the experimental setup (§<a href="#S5.SS1" title="5.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.1</span></a>), then present results comparing <span id="S5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> with off-the-shelf proxies and baselines (§<a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a>). We follow with analysis (§<a href="#S5.SS3" title="5.3 Analysis ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a>), covering different influence estimators, efficiency, factors behind its effectiveness, probe set quality, and ablations. Additional results under varying data budgets, the effect of IPSVD, with diverse candidate training datasets, and sensitivity studies on extreme sparsity and the KL coefficient are provided in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Additional Experiment Results ‣ Appendix ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h4>

<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Datasets and Models.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use the <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dolly</span> dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Conover et al., 2023</a>)</cite> as our candidate training data <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}</annotation></semantics></math> following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2023b</a>)</cite>.
It provides a diverse collection of instruction-response pairs designed for aligning large language models with human preferences. We further evaluate alternative candidate training datasets spanning diverse domains in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Additional Experiment Results ‣ Appendix ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>. We evaluate models ranging from 3B to 7B parameters across four different model families: Llama3.2-3B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dubey et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, Gemma3-4B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, Qwen3-4B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and Qwen2-7B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team, 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>

</section>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Baselines and Evaluation.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To our knowledge, this direction is underexplored, so we mainly compare with off-the-shelf proxies within the same model family.
In addition, we propose two baselines based on related work:
<span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Layer Extraction</span>, which selects layers from the original model using heuristics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Men et al., 2024</a>)</cite>,
and <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Influence Scorer</span>, which trains a smaller model to predict influence scores for the dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, we use MMLU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, BBH <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Suzgun et al., 2022</a>)</cite>,
and TyDiQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Clark et al., 2020</a>)</cite> to evaluate the final performance. Table <a href="#S5.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Datasets and Models. ‣ 5.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> shows some statistics.
Appendix <a href="#A1.SS1" title="A.1 Baseline and Evaluation Details ‣ Appendix A Further Details on Experiment Setup ‣ Appendix ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.1</span></a> contains more details.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Data Selection Settings.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We implement TracIn-based influence estimation following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al. (2024)</a></cite>, adopting the SGD influence variant and omitting the gradient projection component for simplicity. For influence function estimation, we implement it based on the K-FAC method  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grosse and Martens, 2016</a>)</cite>.
The target models are first warmed up on a randomly selected 5% subset of <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}</annotation></semantics></math> for subsequent data selection. Data are then scored according to the computed influence values, and the top 5% are selected. Each model is full fine-tuned on the selected data for 4 epochs. As discussed in Section <a href="#S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3" title="Discussion. ‣ 4.2 Stage 2: Approximate Gradient Alignment in the Weight Space ‣ 4 Proxy Construction via Influence-Preserving Compression ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>, we freeze the embedding and LM head during warm-up to prevent performance degradation and exclude them from influence calculation. Appendix <a href="#A1.SS2" title="A.2 Data Selection Setting Details ‣ Appendix A Further Details on Experiment Setup ‣ Appendix ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2</span></a> contains more details.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Implementation Details.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> is built from the warmed-up target model.
We implement it using 1% of the data source, of which 10% is allocated as probe set, and 90% as aligning data.
We vary the sparsity level <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>, the proportion of parameters removed by compression, to examine the trade-off between efficiency and performance.
Appendix <a href="#A1.SS3" title="A.3 Implementation Details ‣ Appendix A Further Details on Experiment Setup ‣ Appendix ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.3</span></a> contains more details.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span><span id="S5.T2.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> compared with off-the-shelf proxies across four target model families. For each target model, we report results using the full model (shown in gray, provided only as a reference), an off-the-shelf proxy from the same family, and <span id="S5.T2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> with different sparsity levels <math id="S5.T2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>. <span id="S5.T2.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bold</span> and <span id="S5.T2.9" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">underline</span> indicate the best and second-best proxy results, respectively.</figcaption>

<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Main Results</h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first compare <span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> with off-the-shelf proxies, with the results summarized in Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ Implementation Details. ‣ 5.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. We vary <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> so that proxy sizes range from off-the-shelf scale to near the target model.
The key findings are:</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX<span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright"> is effective across different models.</span></span>
<span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> consistently outperforms the off-the-shelf proxies across all sparsity levels on BBH and TyDiQA, while also achieving competitive results on MMLU, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach.
Notably, on Qwen3, <span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> even surpasses the larger 1.7B off-the-shelf proxy with a proxy of only 1.5B parameters.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Larger proxies yield better performance.</span>
Across all four model families, we observe a clear trend: increasing proxy size leads to improved performance. This highlights that our approach enables a controllable trade-off between computational cost and downstream performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Task type matters.</span>
We find that the benefits of <span id="S5.SS2.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> vary across tasks. The performance gains are more pronounced on TyDiQA than on MMLU. We argue that this difference may stem from the nature of the tasks, since TyDiQA and Dolly are both closer to open-domain QA settings, whereas MMLU emphasizes complex reasoning tasks where data selected from Dolly provides only limited improvements. This observation aligns with Eq. <a href="#S4.E4" title="In Proposition 4.1. ‣ 4.1 Stage 1: Influence-Preserving SVD ‣ 4 Proxy Construction via Influence-Preserving Compression ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, which indicates that greater distributional shift between training and validation sets results in a looser error bound.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proxies can even outperform target models.</span>
In some cases, <span id="S5.SS2.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> surpasses the performance obtained with data selected by the target model itself, such as Qwen3-4B with <math id="S5.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.3</annotation></semantics></math> on BBH and Qwen2-7B with <math id="S5.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.3</annotation></semantics></math> on TyDiQA. This phenomenon, where smaller models identify more generalizable training data, has also been reported in prior work across pre-training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Engstrom, 2024</a>)</cite>, fine-tuning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and in-context learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2023a</a>)</cite>. Our experiments reinforce this observation, showing that sometimes proxies can select data for the target model more effectively than the target model itself.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T3" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 3: </span>Comparison of <span id="S5.T3.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> with two baselines: <span id="S5.T3.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Layer Extraction</span> and <span id="S5.T3.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Influence Scorer</span>. For <span id="S5.T3.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> and Layer Extraction, we report the results based on <math id="S5.T3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.3</annotation></semantics></math>. <math id="S5.T3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the performance gain of <span id="S5.T3.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> over the strongest baseline. <span id="S5.T3.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bold</span> indicates the best results.</figcaption>

</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Next, we compare <span id="S5.SS2.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> with two baselines.
As shown in Table <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, <span id="S5.SS2.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> achieves overall stronger performance than both baselines, with an average improvement of 2.81% on Llama3.2-3B and 1.99% on Gemma3-4B. We observe that while the two baselines obtain comparable or slightly higher results on MMLU, these improvements are less conclusive, since both methods perform notably worse than the off-the-shelf proxy on BBH and TyDiQA.
We also acknowledge that both baselines are computationally cheaper, but they do not preserve gradient information and therefore struggle to identify useful data. Additional results on other model families are provided in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Additional Experiment Results ‣ Appendix ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Results on Influence Function.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To validate the effectiveness of <span id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> across different gradient-based influence, we also evaluate <span id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> under the Influence Function. The results are reported in Table <a href="#S5.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 5.3 Analysis ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. We find that <span id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> outperforms off-the-shelf proxies on BBH and TyDiQA while remaining competitive on MMLU. Averaged across tasks, <span id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> achieves clear gains over the smaller proxies on both Llama3.2-3B and Gemma3-4B, leading to a conclusion consistent with Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ Implementation Details. ‣ 5.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. These results suggest that the improvements brought by <span id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> are consistent across different gradient-based influences.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T5" class="ltx_table ltx_align_floatright" style="width:50%;">

</section>
<section id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Efficiency Analysis.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We further analyze the efficiency of <span id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> by reporting both theoretical FLOPs and actual GPU hours.
Figure <a href="#S5.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 5.3 Analysis ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows the FLOPs breakdown on Llama3.2-3B across different sparsity levels. As sparsity increases, the total FLOPs drop substantially, leading to over <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="140" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>140</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">140</annotation></semantics></math> TFLOPs savings at <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho\!=\!0.7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo lspace="0.108em">=</mo><mn>0.7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho\!=\!0.7</annotation></semantics></math> compared to the full 3B model. Moreover, Stage 1 and Stage 2 account for only a small portion of the total FLOPs, and their cost further decreases as sparsity grows.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S5.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ Results on Influence Function. ‣ 5.3 Analysis ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> reports the estimated wall-clock computation measured on a single GH200 GPU, with <span id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> ranging across all sparsity levels from 0.3 to 0.7. Compared to <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>90 minutes required for influence calculation with the 3B model and <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>40 minutes with the 1B off-the-shelf proxy, our method performs influence calculation in only <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>38–44 minutes. Proxy construction (Stage 1 and Stage 2) adds less than 10 minutes of extra cost, bringing the total runtime to about 43–51 minutes. Thus, the efficiency of <span id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> mainly comes from the reduced cost of influence calculation, with proxy construction contributing only a small computational overhead.
Together, these results highlight that <span id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> achieves notable efficiency improvements while maintaining strong performance, making it a practical alternative to direct influence calculation with target models.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T6" class="ltx_table ltx_align_floatright" style="width:50%;">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 6: </span>

</figcaption>

<tr id="S5.T6.10.6" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S5.T6.10.6.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:2.0pt;padding-right:2.0pt;"><span id="S5.T6.10.6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span>, <math id="S5.T6.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.7</annotation></semantics></math></th>
<td id="S5.T6.10.6.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:2.0pt;padding-right:2.0pt;">32.19</td>
<td id="S5.T6.10.6.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:2.0pt;padding-right:2.0pt;"><span id="S5.T6.10.6.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">16.07</span></td>

</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Behind <span id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> Effectiveness.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To understand why <span id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> is effective in data selection, we first examine the similarity between the selected data and the target task using subspace affinity (SA) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Soltanolkotabi et al., 2014</a>)</cite>.
As shown in Table <a href="#S5.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ Efficiency Analysis. ‣ 5.3 Analysis ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, proxies with lower sparsity (e.g., <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.3</annotation></semantics></math>) achieve higher SA than the off-the-shelf 1B proxy, most notably on TyDiQA, suggesting that they capture gradient directions more consistent with the target task.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond similarity, diversity also plays a key role in boosting downstream performance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Therefore, we measure the average nearest-neighbor distance (1-NND) within selected subsets as a measurement for diversity and find that proxies with higher sparsity (e.g., <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.7</annotation></semantics></math>) yield larger 1-NND values than the 1B proxy.
This suggests that even when compressed, <span id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> preserve a sufficient degree of diversity in their selections.
We argue that <span id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> steers selection toward task-relevant directions while its sparsity allows variation in less dominant components, which helps maintain diversity in the selected data.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T7" class="ltx_table ltx_align_floatright" style="width:50%;">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 7: </span>Impact of Probe Set Size. Increasing probe size yields diminishing returns while significantly increasing computational overhead.</figcaption>
