<section id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Probe Set Quality.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We investigate the impact of the probe set configuration on the performance of IProX, specifically focusing on the trade-offs regarding probe set size and data diversity. All experiments in this section are conducted on Llama3.2-3B with a sparsity ratio of <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.7</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We first analyze the sensitivity of proxy performance to the size of the probe set <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math>. As shown in Table <a href="#S5.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ Behind IProX Effectiveness. ‣ 5.3 Analysis ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, there is a clear trade-off between marginal performance gains and computational efficiency. While increasing the probe size to <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p2.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="3\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3\times</annotation></semantics></math> the default value yields performance improvements, these gains saturate around <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p2.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="3\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3\times</annotation></semantics></math>. Notably, further increasing the size to <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p2.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="5\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\times</annotation></semantics></math> results in diminishing returns. From an efficiency perspective, IPSVD benefits from a small <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> to enable fast “skinny SVDs” (Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Efficient Implementation via Probe-Based Approximation and Core SVD ‣ Appendix ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>), and the Stage 1 cost scales roughly linearly with <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math>. Overall, the saturation in performance gains and the increasing Stage 1 cost justify our choice of a moderate default probe size.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T8" class="ltx_table ltx_align_floatright" style="width:55%;">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 8: </span>Impact of Probe Set Diversity. Reducing diversity (via redundancy injection) while keeping size fixed leads to performance degradation.</figcaption>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To assess the role of probe-set diversity, we simulated low-diversity scenarios by replacing 10%–30% of the probe set samples with SMOTE-based interpolation, while strictly keeping the total size <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> fixed.
The results in Table <a href="#S5.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ Probe Set Quality. ‣ 5.3 Analysis ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> demonstrate that performance degrades consistently as diversity decreases. This confirms that IProX benefits significantly from the high diversity naturally provided by our random data and uniform token sampling strategy.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T9" class="ltx_table ltx_align_floatright" style="width:39%;">

<th id="S5.T9.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_r ltx_border_tt" style="padding:0.25pt 5.0pt;"><span id="S5.T9.2.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MMLU</span></th>

</section>
<section id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Ablation Studies.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S5.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ Probe Set Quality. ‣ 5.3 Analysis ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> presents an ablation study on different components.
We observe that removing KL anchoring consistently reduces performance across all three benchmarks, while removing the entire aligning stage leads to even larger drops, particularly on TyDiQA.
The degradation is more pronounced at higher sparsity levels, suggesting that alignment becomes increasingly important as the proxy is more aggressively compressed.
Overall, the results show that KL anchoring and gradient alignment are complementary. KL anchoring stabilizes training by constraining outputs, while gradient alignment preserves influence-relevant directions, and together they maintain the quality of selected data.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h3>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduced <span id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span>, a principled framework for constructing influence-preserving proxies for efficient data selection in LLM fine-tuning. By compressing the target model with an influence-preserving low-rank approximation and refining it through model gradient and output alignment, <span id="S6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> preserves the influence information of the target model while reducing computational cost. Experiments across multiple model families and tasks show consistent gains over off-the-shelf proxies and baselines, together with clear efficiency benefits. These results suggest that influence-preserving proxies offer a scalable approach to gradient-based data selection in LLM fine-tuning.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>

<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_part">Appendix</h2>

<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Further Details on Experiment Setup</h3>

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Baseline and Evaluation Details</h4>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Here, we provide additional implementation details of the baseline and detailed evaluation settings.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ul id="A1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Layer Extraction:</span> We extract layers from the warmed-up target models. Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Men et al. (2024)</a></cite>, each block (i.e., attention + MLP) is scored with an influence defined as:</p>
<table id="A1.Ex4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{\text{LE}}=1-\mathbb{E}_{x}\frac{h_{i}^{\top}h_{i+1}}{\|h_{i}\|\|h_{i+1}\|}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mtext>LE</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{\text{LE}}=1-\mathbb{E}_{x}\frac{h_{i}^{\top}h_{i+1}}{\|h_{i}\|\|h_{i+1}\|},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.I1.i1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A1.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A1.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{i+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{i+1}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the hidden states before and after the <math id="A1.I1.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th block, respectively. This score captures how much the representation changes across the block, with larger values indicating greater influence. For a fair comparison, we set the sparsity to <math id="A1.I1.i1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.3</annotation></semantics></math> and select the top 70% of blocks ranked by their influence scores <math id="A1.I1.i1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{\text{LE}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>I</mi><mtext>LE</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{\text{LE}}</annotation></semantics></math>. The influence is computed using a 1% random sample from <math id="A1.I1.i1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and the final results are reported in Table <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Influence Scorer:</span> Prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2024</a>)</cite> formulates this task as a regression problem, where a smaller model is trained to predict influence scores from a limited set of annotated data. Concretely, the target model is first used to compute influence on a hold-out set, and these values are then used to supervise the smaller model. Once trained, the smaller model is applied to generate influence scores for the entire dataset. This approach raises two concerns. First, it still requires influence computation with the original model to produce annotations. Second, the generalizability of the smaller model is uncertain, as data preferences may shift during training, necessitating repeated re-annotation and retraining for accuracy. In our implementation, we adopt the off-the-shelf model from Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ Implementation Details. ‣ 5.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> as the backbone, attach a regression head, and freeze all other layers during training. For a fair comparison, we use 1% of <math id="A1.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}</annotation></semantics></math> as the hold-out set and perform training only once. The default learning rate is set to <math id="A1.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\mathrm{e}{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\mathrm{e}{-5}</annotation></semantics></math>, and we optimize using Adam with a weight decay of <math id="A1.I1.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\mathrm{e}{-2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\mathrm{e}{-2}</annotation></semantics></math> for 5 epochs.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We follow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al. (2024)</a></cite> to evaluate the performance of the models on the target tasks.
For MMLU, we evaluate 5-shot accuracy on the test set averaged across 57 subtasks. For TyDiQA, we report 1-shot macro-averaged exact match across 9 languages under the gold-passage setting, where a passage containing the reference answer is provided. For BBH, we measure the average 3-shot exact match across all tasks. All models are trained for 4 epochs with a default learning rate of <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\mathrm{e}{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\mathrm{e}{-5}</annotation></semantics></math>, and we report the final performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Data Selection Setting Details</h4>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For TracIn influence, the implementation follows <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al. (2024)</a></cite> with two key modifications. As the experiments are conducted with full fine-tuning rather than parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), the most time-consuming gradient projection step is omitted. The averaged gradient on the validation set is computed and its cosine similarity with the gradient of each training sample is used as the final influence score, rather than Adam moments. In addition, due to computational budget constraints, we warm-up for only one epoch with a default learning rate of <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1e-5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1e-5</annotation></semantics></math> and a weight decay of <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1e-2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1e-2</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For Influence Functions, K-FAC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grosse and Martens, 2016</a>)</cite> is used to compute the inverse Hessian–vector product for each layer, and the resulting vectors are concatenated to form the final representation. For computational efficiency, Hessian statistics are estimated using 1024 samples rather than the entire dataset.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span>Implementation Details</h4>

<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We initialize <span id="A1.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> using 1% of randomly sampled data from <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}</annotation></semantics></math>, allocating 10% to the first stage and 90% to the second stage.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In the first stage, the number of collected second-moment matrices <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> ranges from 512 to 2048, depending on the model size. Rather than averaging over entire sequences to collect <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math>s and <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta</annotation></semantics></math>s, we sample tokens within each sequence, with the sampling budget precomputed to ensure uniform coverage over the entire probe set. This design offers two advantages: (i) random or stratified token sampling better captures local geometry across different positions, difficulty levels, and attention patterns; and (ii) it mitigates length bias. Since sequence lengths vary widely, per-sequence averaging tends to compress the internal diversity of long sequences while disproportionately amplifying or diminishing short sequences.
For numerical stability, we add a damping term of <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{-3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-3}</annotation></semantics></math> when computing the SVD. To improve hardware efficiency, the rank of each layer is further aligned to a multiple of 128, which facilitates optimal tensor core utilization during GPU computation.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For the second stage, we perform a grid search over the following hyperparameters: learning rates of <math id="A1.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\mathrm{e}{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\mathrm{e}{-5}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A1.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5\mathrm{e}{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\mathrm{e}{-5}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="A1.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\mathrm{e}{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\mathrm{e}{-4}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="A1.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{\text{KL}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>λ</mi><mtext>KL</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{\text{KL}}</annotation></semantics></math> values of <math id="A1.SS3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A1.SS3.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.1</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A1.SS3.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.01</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.01</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="A1.SS3.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.001</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.001</annotation></semantics></math>. We use a weight decay of <math id="A1.SS3.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.01</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.01</annotation></semantics></math>, align only the decomposed layers while keeping all others (including biases) fixed, and set the batch size to 4. We use <math id="A1.SS3.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-\cos(\cdot,\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-\cos(\cdot,\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> as the distance metric in Eq <a href="#S4.E6" title="In Aligning Internal Gradient via Low-Rank Projection. ‣ 4.2 Stage 2: Approximate Gradient Alignment in the Weight Space ‣ 4 Proxy Construction via Influence-Preserving Compression ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">All experiments are conducted on compute nodes with ARM architecture and equipped with NVIDIA GH200.</p>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Further Discussion</h3>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Data-centric AI has received increasing attention in recent years <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kang et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kang et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, with data selection emerging as a central paradigm spanning many areas <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ai et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zou et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qi et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zou et al., 2025c</a>)</cite>. Among these approaches, gradient-based methods have become one of the dominant families due to their direct connection to training dynamics and downstream performance. Building on the discussion in the main text (e.g., §<a href="#S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3" title="Discussion. ‣ 4.2 Stage 2: Approximate Gradient Alignment in the Weight Space ‣ 4 Proxy Construction via Influence-Preserving Compression ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>), we further clarify how <span id="A2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> relates to prior work on efficient gradient-based data selection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kwon et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2025c</a>; <a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">At a high level, these lines of work share the same core signal. They treat gradient geometry, such as gradient norms and gradient similarities, as a surrogate for example utility. However, they optimize different parts of the pipeline. Most efficient gradient based selection methods accelerate the selection procedure given access to gradients. Typical strategies reduce the number of scoring steps or checkpoints, compute lower-dimensional or partial gradients, amortize scoring across batches, or use algorithmic approximations to avoid expensive influence computations. Importantly, these approaches still rely on running the original target model to generate the underlying gradients, and mainly reduce the overhead of how gradients are computed, represented, or aggregated for scoring. In contrast, <span id="A2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> targets a complementary bottleneck by reducing the cost of producing gradients. It replaces the full target model with an influence preserving proxy whose forward and backward passes are cheaper, while maintaining the influence relevant gradient signal that downstream selectors depend on. This makes <span id="A2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> orthogonal to algorithmic speedups in the selection rule and naturally composable with them. In practice, one can run a lightweight selector on top of a <span id="A2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> proxy and obtain multiplicative gains by reducing both the per gradient cost and the number or dimensionality of gradient evaluations required by the selector.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Despite these benefits, <span id="A2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> also has limitations that mirror the assumptions behind influence-based approximations. Aggressive compression can compound approximation errors across layers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ai et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>. While our alignment stage mitigates this effect, there remains an inherent trade-off between proxy efficiency and the truthfulness of gradient signals used for selection. In addition, our proxy construction is intrinsically layer-wise, so in sufficiently deep networks, small layer-level mismatches may accumulate as they propagate through the model. This effect may be more noticeable under stochastic fine-tuning dynamics, where noise in optimization can interact with approximation error and lead to modest deviations in per example scores or selection rankings.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">

<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Additional Results Compared with Baseline Methods</h5>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We extend the comparison of <span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> with baselines to two target models, Qwen3-4B and Qwen2-7B, under the TracIn influence. The results are summarized in Table <a href="#A3.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ Appendix C Additional Experiment Results ‣ Appendix ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>. We observe that the trends in Table <a href="#A3.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ Appendix C Additional Experiment Results ‣ Appendix ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> are consistent with those reported in Table <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, confirming that <span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> consistently outperforms the baselines across different target models and tasks. In particular, the gains on TyDiQA are especially notable, with <span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> improving by <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+3.85" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>3.85</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+3.85</annotation></semantics></math> on Qwen3-4B and <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+7.84" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>7.84</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+7.84</annotation></semantics></math> on Qwen2-7B compared to the strongest baseline. These improvements highlight that the influence-preserving design of <span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> is more effective at capturing task-relevant gradients than heuristic or predictive alternatives. Moreover, the consistency of the results across both medium-size and large-size models suggests that the advantages of <span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> generalize beyond a single model family, further reinforcing its effectiveness and scalability for gradient-based data selection.</p>
</div>

<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Effect of Data Budgets.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A3.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ Additional Results Compared with Baseline Methods ‣ Appendix C Additional Experiment Results ‣ Appendix ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> reports the evaluation results of <span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> under two different data budgets, 1% and 20%. In both cases, <span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">IProX</span> consistently outperforms the off-the-shelf 1B proxy, demonstrating its effectiveness regardless of the amount of data used for selection. However, we also find that the 20% budget leads to noticeable degradation, particularly on TyDiQA. This decline can be attributed to the inclusion of redundant or noisy samples at higher budgets, which dilutes the benefits of high-quality data and increases the risk of overfitting. Similar observations have been reported in prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, further underscoring the importance of data selection.</p>
</div>

<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Ablation of IPSVD.</h5>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To isolate the contribution of the second-moment reweighting in IPSVD, we conduct an ablation study where we replace IPSVD with standard SVD while keeping all other components unchanged. As shown in Table <a href="#A3.T12" title="Table 12 ‣ Effect of Data Budgets. ‣ Appendix C Additional Experiment Results ‣ Appendix ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>, replacing IPSVD with standard SVD leads to consistent performance degradation across all sparsity levels and benchmarks. The average score drops by approximately 2 to 3 points, with the most severe decline observed on TyDiQA (up to 6 points). These results empirically confirm that standard SVD, which minimizes output reconstruction error, is insufficient for preserving gradient-based influence, thereby validating the necessity of the reweighting strategy employed in IPSVD.</p>
</div>
</section>

</figure>
<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To further validate the robustness of IProX across distinct task formats and domain shifts, we extend our evaluation to two additional training datasets: CoT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2022</a>)</cite> and BioInstruct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tran et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. For a fair comparison, we keep the total size of the candidate training data fixed by randomly sampling the same number of samples.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A3.T13" title="Table 13 ‣ Diverse Candidate Training Data. ‣ Appendix C Additional Experiment Results ‣ Appendix ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a> summarizes the performance of Llama3.2-3B proxies constructed via IProX compared to baselines. IProX consistently outperforms the off-the-shelf 1B proxy and remains competitive with the full 3B model on both new datasets.
We also observe distinct behaviors arising from domain shifts. Training on BioInstruct leads to noticeable degradation on general benchmarks (MMLU, TyDiQA), likely due to the distribution shift towards specialized biomedical content. However, the performance drop on BBH is mild, consistent with the partial overlap between BioInstruct and the biomedical subsets within BBH. Conversely, training on CoT tends to improve performance across all benchmarks. Most notably, we observe significant gains on TyDiQA, suggesting that the reasoning-focused supervision in CoT data transfers effectively to other complex tasks.</p>
</div>
</section>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We investigate the behavior of IProX under extreme compression scenarios (<math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.9</annotation></semantics></math>). While SVD-based approximations naturally face limitations in this regime due to the significant reduction in rank, we aim to determine if IProX retains utility compared to heuristic baselines.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A3.T14" title="Table 14 ‣ Performance under Extreme Compression ‣ Appendix C Additional Experiment Results ‣ Appendix ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a> compares IProX against Layer Extraction on both Llama3.2-3B and Qwen2-7B at 90% sparsity. Although performance naturally degrades compared to lower sparsity settings, IProX consistently outperforms the Layer Extraction baseline across all metrics. The degradation is relatively mild, and the performance gap highlights that even in extreme regimes, our method preserves influence information more effectively than simple heuristic alternatives.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">The Sensitivity of KL Coefficient</h5>

</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We analyze the sensitivity of IProX to the KL divergence coefficient (<math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma_{\text{KL}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>γ</mi><mtext>KL</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma_{\text{KL}}</annotation></semantics></math>) used in the alignment objective. The KL term provides essential anchoring for stability, preventing the proxy from drifting too far from the target model’s output distribution.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A3.T15" title="Table 15 ‣ The Sensitivity of KL Coefficient ‣ Appendix C Additional Experiment Results ‣ Appendix ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a> presents the results on Llama3.2-3B with a sparsity ratio of <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=0.7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=0.7</annotation></semantics></math>. We observe that performance degrades if <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma_{\text{KL}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>γ</mi><mtext>KL</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma_{\text{KL}}</annotation></semantics></math> is set too high (<math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.5</annotation></semantics></math>), as the distillation loss begins to overpower the influence alignment objective. Conversely, values that are too low (<math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\leq 0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mn>0.01</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\leq 0.01</annotation></semantics></math>) provide insufficient regularization, leading to suboptimal retention of the target model’s capabilities. Based on these findings, we adopt a moderate value of <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma_{\text{KL}}=0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>γ</mi><mtext>KL</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma_{\text{KL}}=0.1</annotation></semantics></math> for our main experiments.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Proof of Proposition <a href="#S4.Thmtheorem1" title="Proposition 4.1. ‣ 4.1 Stage 1: Influence-Preserving SVD ‣ 4 Proxy Construction via Influence-Preserving Compression ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a></h3>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Here, we provide a complete proof for Proposition <a href="#S4.Thmtheorem1" title="Proposition 4.1. ‣ 4.1 Stage 1: Influence-Preserving SVD ‣ 4 Proxy Construction via Influence-Preserving Compression ‣ Influence-Preserving Proxies for Gradient-Based Data Selection in LLM Fine-tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>. We fix a layer <math id="A4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> and a perturbation <math id="A4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> to its weight matrix <math id="A4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math>, such that the perturbed weight is <math id="A4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widehat{W}_{\ell}=W_{\ell}+E_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>W</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widehat{W}_{\ell}=W_{\ell}+E_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The influence contribution of layer <math id="A4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> and the layer-local directional effect are defined as:</p>

<p id="A4.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{\ell-1}(z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{\ell-1}(z)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta_{\ell}(z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta_{\ell}(z)</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the input and the upstream gradient at the layer <math id="A4.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math>.
We begin by stating the technical assumptions required for our result, which are similar to simplifying assumptions often adopted in theoretical studies of deep neural networks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Virmaux and Scaman, 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Frei et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ol id="A4.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="A4.I1.ix1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="A4.I1.ix1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(A1)</span></span> 
<div id="A4.I1.ix1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.I1.ix1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.I1.ix1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(Backward Smoothness).</span> For almost every sample <math id="A4.I1.ix1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math>, the map <math id="A4.I1.ix1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u\mapsto\delta_{\ell}(z;u)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">↦</mo><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u\mapsto\delta_{\ell}(z;u)</annotation></semantics></math> is differentiable in a neighborhood of the unperturbed pre-activation <math id="A4.I1.ix1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{\ell}(z)=W_{\ell}h(z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{\ell}(z)=W_{\ell}h(z)</annotation></semantics></math>. There exists a measurable function <math id="A4.I1.ix1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K(z)\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K(z)\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math> such that the Jacobian <math id="A4.I1.ix1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{u}\delta_{\ell}(z;u)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{u}\delta_{\ell}(z;u)</annotation></semantics></math> satisfies <math id="A4.I1.ix1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|D_{u}\delta_{\ell}(z;u)\|_{\text{op}}\leq K(z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mtext>op</mtext></msub><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|D_{u}\delta_{\ell}(z;u)\|_{\text{op}}\leq K(z)</annotation></semantics></math> uniformly for <math id="A4.I1.ix1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math> along the line segment <math id="A4.I1.ix1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{u_{\ell}(z)+\tau E_{\ell}h(z):\tau\in[0,1]\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo rspace="0.278em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{u_{\ell}(z)+\tau E_{\ell}h(z):\tau\in[0,1]\}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A4.I1.ix2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="A4.I1.ix2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(A2)</span></span> 
<div id="A4.I1.ix2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.I1.ix2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.I1.ix2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(Finite Second Moments).</span> The expectations <math id="A4.I1.ix2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}\|h_{\ell}(z)\|^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}\|h_{\ell}(z)\|^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A4.I1.ix2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}\|\delta_{\ell}(z)\|^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}\|\delta_{\ell}(z)\|^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A4.I1.ix2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}\|h_{\ell}(z^{\prime})\|^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}\|h_{\ell}(z^{\prime})\|^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A4.I1.ix2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}\|\delta_{\ell}(z^{\prime})\|^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}\|\delta_{\ell}(z^{\prime})\|^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> are all finite for an independent copy <math id="A4.I1.ix2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A4.I1.ix3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="A4.I1.ix3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(A3)</span></span> 
<div id="A4.I1.ix3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.I1.ix3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.I1.ix3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(Coherence of Local Directions).</span> There exists a constant <math id="A4.I1.ix3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta\in(0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta\in(0,1]</annotation></semantics></math> such that for almost every <math id="A4.I1.ix3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A4.I1.ix3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\langle\delta_{\ell}(z),E_{\ell}h_{\ell}(z)\rangle|\geq\eta\|\delta_{\ell}(z)\|\|E_{\ell}h_{\ell}(z)\|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\langle\delta_{\ell}(z),E_{\ell}h_{\ell}(z)\rangle|\geq\eta\|\delta_{\ell}(z)\|\|E_{\ell}h_{\ell}(z)\|</annotation></semantics></math>. This implies the cosine of the angle between <math id="A4.I1.ix3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta(z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta(z)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A4.I1.ix3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{\ell}h(z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{\ell}h(z)</annotation></semantics></math> is bounded away from zero.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A4.I1.ix4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item"><span id="A4.I1.ix4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(A4)</span></span> 
<div id="A4.I1.ix4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.I1.ix4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.I1.ix4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(Bounded Covariate Shift).</span> The distributions of <math id="A4.I1.ix4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A4.I1.ix4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> are such that there exists a constant <math id="A4.I1.ix4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math> satisfying <math id="A4.I1.ix4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}_{z^{\prime}}[e_{\ell}(z^{\prime})^{2}]\leq\kappa\mathbb{E}_{z}[e_{\ell}(z)^{2}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>z</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}_{z^{\prime}}[e_{\ell}(z^{\prime})^{2}]\leq\kappa\mathbb{E}_{z}[e_{\ell}(z)^{2}]</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="A4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">With these assumptions in place, we can state the following proposition.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_proposition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="A4.Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proposition D.1</span></span><span id="A4.Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="A4.Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Under Assumptions (A1)-(A4), for any perturbation <math id="A4.Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math>, there exists a finite, data-dependent constant <math id="A4.Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{\kappa}&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>κ</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{\kappa}&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> such that:</span></p>
<table id="A4.E9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A4.E9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}_{z,z^{\prime}}\big|I_{\widehat{W}_{\ell}}(z,z^{\prime})-I_{W_{\ell}}(z,z^{\prime})\big|\;\leq\;C_{\kappa}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{z}\!\left[e_{\ell}(z)^{2}\right]}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" stretchy="true">|</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>W</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" rspace="0.280em" stretchy="true">|</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.558em">≤</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>κ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>z</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}_{z,z^{\prime}}\big|I_{\widehat{W}_{\ell}}(z,z^{\prime})-I_{W_{\ell}}(z,z^{\prime})\big|\;\leq\;C_{\kappa}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{z}\!\left[e_{\ell}(z)^{2}\right]}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(9)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div id="A4.2" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="A4.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text">Let <math id="A4.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\ell}(\tau)=W_{\ell}+\tau E_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\ell}(\tau)=W_{\ell}+\tau E_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="A4.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>. Define <math id="A4.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi(\tau;z,z^{\prime})\triangleq I_{W_{\ell}(\tau)}(z,z^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≜</mo><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi(\tau;z,z^{\prime})\triangleq I_{W_{\ell}(\tau)}(z,z^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math>. The input <math id="A4.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h(z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h(z)</annotation></semantics></math> does not depend on <math id="A4.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math>, so the dependence on <math id="A4.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> enters only through <math id="A4.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta_{\ell}(z;u_{\ell}(\tau,z))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta_{\ell}(z;u_{\ell}(\tau,z))</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="A4.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{\ell}(\tau,z)=W_{\ell}(\tau)h(z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{\ell}(\tau,z)=W_{\ell}(\tau)h(z)</annotation></semantics></math>.
We can represent the change in influence as:</span></p>
<table id="A4.Ex6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A4.Ex6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{\widehat{W}_{\ell}}(z,z^{\prime})-I_{W_{\ell}}(z,z^{\prime})=\int_{0}^{1}\phi^{\prime}(\tau;z,z^{\prime})\,d\tau." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>W</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mrow><msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{\widehat{W}_{\ell}}(z,z^{\prime})-I_{W_{\ell}}(z,z^{\prime})=\int_{0}^{1}\phi^{\prime}(\tau;z,z^{\prime})\,d\tau.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A4.p4.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.p4.2.1" class="ltx_text">Differentiating <math id="A4.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> with respect to <math id="A4.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> gives:</span></p>
<table id="A4.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A4.Ex7"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A4.Ex7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\phi^{\prime}(\tau;z,z^{\prime})=" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\phi^{\prime}(\tau;z,z^{\prime})=</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A4.Ex7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\left\langle\frac{d}{d\tau}\delta_{\ell}(z;u_{\ell}(\tau,z)),\delta_{\ell}(z^{\prime};u_{\ell}(\tau,z^{\prime}))\right\rangle_{F}\langle h_{\ell}(z),h_{\ell}(z^{\prime})\rangle_{F}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mrow><mo>⟨</mo><mrow><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>δ</mi><mi </table>
<p id="A4.p5.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.p5.4.1" class="ltx_text">Now, we invoke the bounded covariate shift from Assumption (A4), which implies <math id="A4.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{z^{\prime}}[e_{\ell}(z^{\prime})^{2}]}\leq\sqrt{\kappa}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{z}[e_{\ell}(z)^{2}]}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msqrt><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></msqrt><mo>≤</mo><mrow><msqrt><mi>κ</mi></msqrt><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>z</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{z^{\prime}}[e_{\ell}(z^{\prime})^{2}]}\leq\sqrt{\kappa}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{z}[e_{\ell}(z)^{2}]}</annotation></semantics></math>. This allows us to bound the entire expression in terms of the expectation over <math id="A4.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math>:</span></p>

</table>
<p id="A4.p5.5" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.p5.5.1" class="ltx_text">By defining <math id="A4.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{\kappa}\triangleq C+C^{\prime}\sqrt{\kappa}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>κ</mi></msub><mo>≜</mo><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><msup><mi>C</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><mi>κ</mi></msqrt></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{\kappa}\triangleq C+C^{\prime}\sqrt{\kappa}</annotation></semantics></math>, which is a finite, data-dependent constant, we arrive at the desired result:</span></p>

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A4.Ex21.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}_{z,z^{\prime}}\big|I_{\widehat{W}_{\ell}}(z,z^{\prime})-I_{W_{\ell}}(z,z^{\prime})\big|\;\leq\;C_{\kappa}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{z}\!\left[e_{\ell}(z)^{2}\right]}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" stretchy="true">|</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>W</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>W</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" rspace="0.280em" stretchy="true">|</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.558em">≤</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>κ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mi>z</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}_{z,z^{\prime}}\big|I_{\widehat{W}_{\ell}}(z,z^{\prime})-I_{W_{\ell}}(z,z^{\prime})\big|\;\leq\;C_{\kappa}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{z}\!\left[e_{\ell}(z)^{2}\right]}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
